claims.claim: Self-pMHCs generally outnumber foreign-pMHCs by several orders of magnitude.
claims.source: Compounding this challenge, self-pMHCs generally outnumber foreign-pMHCs by several orders of magnitude (Unternaehrer et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2003; Bhardwaj et al., 1993; Irvine et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claims.claim: For many cell surface receptors, occupancy drives the strength of signaling.
claims.source: For many cell surface receptors, occupancy drives the strength of signaling. Lower affinity ligands can signal as well as high affinity ligands when their concentration is increased such that an equal number of receptors are bound (Kinzer-Ursem et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a general principle in cell signaling supported by citation.

claims.claim: Low affinity pMHCs are significantly less potent than high affinity pMHCs, even when adjusted for occupancy.
claims.source: This is unlikely to be the case for activation of the T cell, because low affinity pMHCs are significantly less potent than high affinity pMHCs, even when adjusted for occupancy (Daniels et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: More TCRs are likely bound to self-pMHC than foreign-pMHC given the large excess of self-pMHC and relatively small differences in binding affinity.
claims.source: Furthermore, given the large excess of self-pMHC (Unternaehrer et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2003; Bhardwaj et al., 1993; Irvine et al., 2002) and the relatively small differences in binding affinity (Davis et al., 1998; Germain and Stefanová, 1999; Gascoigne et al., 2001), it is likely that more TCRs are bound to self-pMHC than foreign-pMHC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited quantitative data about pMHC abundance and binding affinities.

claims.claim: Kinetic proofreading predicts that small differences in ligand binding half-life can be amplified into large differences in signaling.
claims.source: A major model of T cell ligand discrimination is kinetic proofreading (McKeithan, 1995), which predicts that small differences in ligand binding half-life can be amplified into large differences in signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the kinetic proofreading model cited.

claims.claim: Kinetic proofreading allows a few receptors bound to long-lived ligands to signal better than many receptors bound to short-lived ligands.
claims.source: Such a model is attractive because it allows a few receptors bound to long-lived ligands to signal better than many receptors bound to short-lived ligands, potentially explaining why abundant self-pMHCs do not activate T cells, though scarce foreign-pMHCs do.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the kinetic proofreading model.

claims.claim: Kinetic proofreading posits a delay made up of multiple irreversible biochemical steps between ligand binding and downstream signaling.
claims.source: It posits a delay made up of multiple irreversible biochemical steps between ligand binding and downstream signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the kinetic proofreading mechanism.

claims.claim: In kinetic proofreading, only ligands that bind persistently signal effectively.
claims.source: Only ligands that bind persistently signal effectively.
claims.evidence: This is a key prediction of the kinetic proofreading model.

claims.claim: In kinetic proofreading, biochemical steps only occur while the ligand is bound and quickly reset upon dissociation.
claims.source: These steps only occur while the ligand is bound and quickly reset upon dissociation, preventing two successive short binding events from mimicking one long binding event.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic feature of the kinetic proofreading model.

claims.claim: Kinetic proofreading gives DNA replication, protein translation, and mRNA splicing specificity far beyond what would be predicted from equilibrium binding constants alone.
claims.source: This mechanism is based on the kinetic proofreading that gives DNA replication, protein translation (Ninio, 1975; Hopfield, 1974), and mRNA splicing (Burgess and Guthrie, 1993) specificity far beyond what would be predicted from equilibrium binding constants alone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on kinetic proofreading in other biological systems.

claims.claim: Stimulatory pMHCs generally have longer binding half-lives, while non-stimulatory pMHCs have shorter binding half-lives.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, kinetic measurements generally show that stimulatory pMHCs have longer binding half-lives, while non-stimulatory pMHCs have shorter binding half-lives (Davis et al., 1998; Germain and Stefanová, 1999; Gascoigne et al., 2001; Matsui et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Recent techniques that measure pMHC binding affinities in more native 2D environments show a larger range of binding affinities than previously measured.
claims.source: However, recent techniques that measure pMHC binding affinities in more native 2D environments show a larger range of binding affinities than previously measured (Huang et al., 2010), suggesting that there may not be as large an excess of self-pMHC bound to the TCR and raises the question of the magnitude of kinetic proofreading needed to discriminate pMHC ligands.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claims.claim: When the binding interface is altered in altered peptide series, both the bond's half-life and stability under tension must change together.
claims.source: The limitation of this approach is that when the binding interface is altered, both the bond's half-life and stability under tension must change together (Figure 1A, left).
claims.evidence: This is a biophysical constraint illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The TCR is mechanosensitive.
claims.source: Differentiating the effects of these two variables is essential because recent evidence has shown that the TCR is mechanosenstive (Kim et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2017; Das et al., 2015) and that foreign-pMHC can form catch bonds with the TCR, growing more stable under load (Liu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: Foreign-pMHC can form catch bonds with the TCR, growing more stable under load.
claims.source: Differentiating the effects of these two variables is essential because recent evidence has shown that the TCR is mechanosenstive (Kim et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2017; Das et al., 2015) and that foreign-pMHC can form catch bonds with the TCR, growing more stable under load (Liu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: LOVTRAP is one of the few optogenetic systems where light stimulates the dissociation of two proteins on the order of seconds.
claims.source: We chose the LOVTRAP system for optogenetic control of bind half-life because it is one of the few systems where light stimulates the dissociation of two proteins on the order of seconds (Ni et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2016), the approximate physiologic range of pMHC-TCR interactions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on LOVTRAP.

claims.claim: The approximate physiologic range of pMHC-TCR interactions is on the order of seconds.
claims.source: We chose the LOVTRAP system for optogenetic control of bind half-life because it is one of the few systems where light stimulates the dissociation of two proteins on the order of seconds (Ni et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2016), the approximate physiologic range of pMHC-TCR interactions.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR-pMHC binding kinetics.

claims.claim: Zdk preferentially binds LOV2 in the dark but quickly unbinds when a photon of blue light excites LOV2, inducing a conformational change.
claims.source: LOVTRAP consists of two parts: a blue-light sensitive protein (LOV2) and an engineered binding partner (Zdk). Zdk preferentially binds LOV2 in the dark but quickly unbinds when a photon of blue light excites LOV2, inducing a conformational change.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the LOVTRAP mechanism based on prior characterization.

claims.claim: Low photon fluxes enforce longer binding half-lives while high photon fluxes enforce shorter binding half-lives in the LOVTRAP system.
claims.source: Since photons of blue light stimulate Zdk dissociation, low photon fluxes enforce longer binding half-lives while high photon fluxes enforce shorter binding half-lives.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the LOVTRAP mechanism.

claims.claim: The intrinsic kinetics of Zdk dissociation from the ground and excited states of LOV2 set the achievable half-life range to approximately 500 ms to 10 s.
claims.source: The intrinsic kinetics of Zdk dissociation from the ground and excited states of LOV2 set the upper and lower bounds on the range of achievable half-lives (approximately 500 ms to 10 s in our hands; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is measured experimentally as shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The CAR approach is simpler than the TCR, easier to engineer, and medically relevant.
claims.source: To construct our synthetic ligand-receptor pair, we used a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) approach, which has the advantage of being simpler than the TCR, easier to engineer, and medically relevant in its own right (Barrett et al., 2014; Sadelain et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a general characterization of CARs supported by citations.

claims.claim: CARs minimally consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain, a transmembrane domain and an intracellular signaling domain.
claims.source: CARs minimally consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain, a transmembrane domain and an intracellular signaling domain.
claims.evidence: This is a standard definition of CAR structure.

claims.claim: The optogenetic approach allows testing of the kinetic proofreading model directly by uncoupling binding half-life from bond stability under tension.
claims.source: A key advantage of this approach is that it allows us to test the kinetic proofreading model directly. For most protein-protein interactions, the binding half-life and the bond's stability under tension necessarily co-vary with each other, as they are both consequences of the height of the transition state. This makes it hard to distinguish between a kinetic proofreading and mechanosensitive model of T cell signaling. A ligand with a long binding half-life is necessarily more stable under load, and both models predict it would be more stimulatory. Our approach uncouples these parameters by using one ligand-receptor pair to explore a range of half-lives.
claims.evidence: This is a key conceptual advantage of the approach, based on biophysical principles.

claims.claim: Blue light, not point mutations, tunes the binding half-life in the optogenetic approach.
claims.source: Blue light, not point mutations, tunes the binding half-life.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: Because the ligand-receptor pair remains constant in all experiments, the amount of tension they can withstand also remains constant.
claims.source: Because the ligand-receptor pair remains constant in all experiments, so too does the amount of tension they can withstand.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of keeping the binding interface constant.

claims.claim: The synthetic CAR approach helps bypass some early signaling steps such as CD4 or CD8 coreceptor involvement.
claims.source: An advantage of our synthetic CAR approach is that it is simpler than the TCR, helping to bypass some early signaling steps (e.g. CD4 or CD8 coreceptor involvement which are lacking in the CAR; Harris and Kranz, 2016) and focus on the role the shared downstream pathway can play in ligand discrimination.
claims.evidence: This is a characteristic of the CAR system supported by citation.

claims.claim: Longer binding lifetimes are a key parameter for potent T cell signaling.
claims.source: By directly controlling ligand binding half-life with light and holding all other binding parameters constant, we show that longer binding lifetimes are a key parameter for potent T cell signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion supported by the experimental data showing DAG levels increase with binding half-life.

claims.claim: Ligand discrimination occurs in the proximal signaling pathway, downstream of ZAP70 recruitment and upstream of DAG accumulation.
claims.source: Surprisingly, this discrimination occurs in the proximal signaling pathway, downstream of ZAP70 recruitment and upstream of DAG accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing ZAP70 recruitment is independent of half-life while DAG is dependent on half-life.

claims.claim: LOV2 accumulated under cells in the absence of blue light and dispersed following illumination with blue light.
claims.source: As expected, LOV2 accumulated under the cells in the absence of blue light and dispersed following illumination with blue light (Figure 1C, Video 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Blue light drives multiple cycles of LOV2 binding and unbinding without apparent loss of potency.
claims.source: Blue light drives multiple cycles of binding and unbinding without apparent loss of potency (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the time course data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Binding of the LOV2 ligand induces DAG accumulation in cells.
claims.source: DAG levels spiked and cells spread onto the SLBs in a blue-light-gated fashion (Figure 1C,E and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy data shown in Figure 1C,E and Video 3.

claims.claim: No blue-light-dependent changes in DAG levels were observed when LOV2 was omitted from the bilayer.
claims.source: We observed no blue-light-dependent changes in DAG levels when LOV2 was omitted from the bilayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a negative control shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: ZAP70 co-localized to sites of CAR occupancy.
claims.source: Additionally, a ZAP70-mCherry reporter co-localized well to sites of CAR occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: DAG showed roughly diffuse localization throughout the cell, consistent with its diffusion away from sites of production.
claims.source: DAG showed roughly diffuse localization throughout the cell, consistent with its diffusion away from sites of production (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is observed in microscopy images and is consistent with known DAG behavior.

claims.claim: Both CAR occupancy and DAG levels rise around 30 s after removing blue light.
claims.source: While the slow dark reversion of LOV2 prevents true acute stimulation of our cells, both CAR occupancy and DAG levels rise around 30 s after removing blue light (Video 2, Video 3), consistent with DAG production beginning within seconds of receptor engagement.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the time course videos.

claims.claim: The CAR was expressed at between 62–238 × 10³ molecules on the cell surface.
claims.source: The CAR was expressed at between 62–238 × 103 molecules on the cell surface, which is slightly lower but comparable to the native TCR complex in Jurkats (273–547 × 103 molecules; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is measured by flow cytometry as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The native TCR complex in Jurkats is expressed at 273–547 × 10³ molecules on the cell surface.
claims.source: The CAR was expressed at between 62–238 × 103 molecules on the cell surface, which is slightly lower but comparable to the native TCR complex in Jurkats (273–547 × 103 molecules; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is measured by flow cytometry as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Cells were sensitive to between ~40–1,200 LOV2 molecules/um² on the bilayer.
claims.source: Cells were sensitive to between ~40–1,200 LOV2 molecules/um2 on the bilayer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Methods), which is comparable in sensitivity to other CARs with precisely tunable ligands (Taylor et al., 2017) and slightly less sensitive than primary T cell presented with pMHCs on SLBs (Manz et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is measured experimentally and compared to prior work via citations.

claims.claim: Within the same field of view, cells could have high or low-to-undetectable receptor occupancies but similar DAG levels when exposed to similar doses of blue light.
claims.source: We noticed that within the same field of view, cells could have high or low-to-undetectable receptor occupancies (red and white arrows, respectively; Figure 1C,D). However, despite clear differences in receptor occupancy, all cells had similar DAG levels when exposed to similar doses of blue light (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the microscopy data shown in Figure 1C,D,E.

claims.claim: Increasing blue-light intensities increased Zdk dissociation and tuned the effective binding half-life from ten seconds to approximately 500 ms.
claims.source: Increasing blue-light intensities increased Zdk dissociation and tuned the effective binding half-life from ten seconds to approximately 500 ms (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is measured in vitro as shown in Figure 2A,B.

claims.claim: Manipulating blue light levels finely tuned DAG levels and receptor occupancy.
claims.source: In addition to providing control over binding half-life, manipulating the blue light levels also finely tuned DAG levels and receptor occupancy (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Video 6 and Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the time course data in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: At constant receptor occupancy, increasing ligand binding half-life increases DAG signaling.
claims.source: Conducting multiple experiments with different LOV2 concentrations and gating the data over a narrow range of receptor occupancy shows a clear result: increasing ligand binding half-life increases DAG levels, despite cells having near identical receptor occupancy (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analyzing data across different LOV2 concentrations at constant occupancy, shown in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: Signaling increases the most for binding half-lives between 4–7 s.
claims.source: Intriguingly, signaling increases the most for binding half-lives between 4–7 s, in close agreement with previous estimates of the binding half-life threshold for stimulatory versus non-stimulatory pMHCs (O'Donoghue et al., 2013; Palmer and Naeher, 2009; Huppa et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the data and compared to prior estimates via citations.

claims.claim: Fast rebinding can make ligands stimulatory by extending the effective engagement time of the receptor.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that fast rebinding can also make ligands stimulatory by extending the effective engagement time of the receptor (Aleksic et al., 2010; Govern et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: 2D kinetic measurements show much wider ranges of on-rates than off-rates in the OT-I system.
claims.source: Interestingly, 2D kinetic measurements show much wider ranges of on-rates than off-rates in the OT-I system (Huang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claims.claim: The effects of ligand rebinding are anticipated to be reduced in the optogenetic approach compared with an altered peptide series because LOV2 is refractory to CAR binding after being stimulated with blue light.
claims.source: However, we anticipate the effects of ligand rebinding to be reduced in our approach compared with an altered peptide series, as LOV2 is refractory to CAR binding after being stimulated with blue light.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of LOV2.

claims.claim: The enforced ligand binding half-life predicted DAG levels well, regardless of the amount of ligand present.
claims.source: Strikingly, the enforced ligand binding half-life predicted DAG levels well, regardless of the amount of ligand present. When DAG is plotted as a function of binding half-life, the response curves from different experiments nearly overlap with each other, showing a strong correlation coefficient (Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, top).
claims.evidence: This is shown by analyzing data across different LOV2 concentrations in Figure 3D,E.

claims.claim: DAG plotted as a function of receptor occupancy shows a poor correlation.
claims.source: By contrast, plotting DAG as a function of receptor occupancy shows a poor correlation (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Binding half-life is a major determinant of CAR signaling.
claims.source: Because half-life is a strong predictor of DAG levels across a range of receptor occupancies, these data argue that binding half-life is a major determinant of CAR signaling.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the correlation analysis of DAG with half-life versus occupancy.

claims.claim: The degree of kinetic proofreading (n) is 2.7 ± 0.5 (95% CI).
claims.source: Fitting our data, we find n = 2.7 ± 0.5 (95% CI; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2)which means this degree of proofreading could allow T cells to amplify a 10-fold difference in ligand binding half-life into a ~ 5,000 fold difference in DAG levels.
claims.evidence: This is calculated by fitting the data to a kinetic proofreading model as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claims.claim: A degree of proofreading of n = 2.7 could allow T cells to amplify a 10-fold difference in ligand binding half-life into a ~5,000 fold difference in DAG levels.
claims.source: Fitting our data, we find n = 2.7 ± 0.5 (95% CI; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2)which means this degree of proofreading could allow T cells to amplify a 10-fold difference in ligand binding half-life into a ~ 5,000 fold difference in DAG levels.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the fitted model parameter n.

claims.claim: ZAP70 recruitment showed no detectable evidence of kinetic proofreading.
claims.source: We addressed this question by measuring one of the earliest signaling events: the recruitment of ZAP70 to the CAR. ZAP70 binds to doubly phosphorylated immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITMAs) in the CAR's cytoplasmic domain. In contrast to DAG levels, ZAP70 recruitment showed no detectable evidence of kinetic proofreading (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claims.claim: ZAP70 recruitment was solely dependent on CAR occupancy and was unaffected by the ligand binding half-life.
claims.source: In other words, ZAP70 recruitment was solely dependent on CAR occupancy and was unaffected by the ligand binding half-life.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the ZAP70 recruitment data showing n ≈ 0.

claims.claim: The observed kinetic proofreading occurs somewhere downstream of ZAP70 recruitment and upstream of DAG production.
claims.source: As live cell reporters reflect the cumulative effect of all upstream signaling steps, these results argue that the observed kinetic proofreading occurs somewhere downstream of ZAP70 recruitment and upstream of DAG production.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of ZAP70 recruitment (no proofreading) versus DAG levels (proofreading).

claims.claim: T cells adhered to a supported lipid bilayer can display ligand-independent signaling.
claims.source: It is important to recognize how cell adhesion can affect cell signaling, as T cells adhered to a supported lipid bilayer can display ligand-independent signaling (Chang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The close (<20 nm) apposition of the two membranes can exclude the bulky transmembrane phosphatase CD45 away from CARs or TCRs, favoring ITAM phosphorylation and T cell signaling.
claims.source: The close (<20 nm) apposition of the two membranes can exclude the bulky transmembrane phosphatase CD45 away from the more homogenously distributed CARs or TCRs, favoring ITAM phosphorylation and T cell signaling (Chang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: An equal degree of proofreading at the level of DAG is observed whether or not passive adhesion was used (n = 2.7 ± 0.5 with anti-β2m versus n = 2.8 ± 0.2 without anti-β2m).
claims.source: We observe an equal degree of proofreading at the level of DAG whether or not passive adhesion was used (n = 2.7 ± 0.5 with anti-β2m versus n = 2.8 ± 0.2 without anti-β2m [Figure 4—figure supplement 3]; 95% CI).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing data sets with and without the anti-β2m antibody.

claims.claim: CD45 exclusion does not contribute to measurable kinetic proofreading at the level of ZAP70 recruitment in the CAR system.
claims.source: While we did not measure CD45 localization, our results suggest that CD45 exclusion does not contribute to measurable kinetic proofreading at the level of ZAP70 recruitment in our CAR system.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ZAP70 recruitment shows no proofreading.

claims.claim: CD45's contribution to kinetic proofreading may be different in the context of the native TCR-pMHC interaction because CD45 exclusion and T cell signaling are sensitive to the size of the extracellular domains.
claims.source: However, because CD45 exclusion and T cell signaling are sensitive to the size of the extracellular domains (Chang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2018; Irles et al., 2003; James and Vale, 2012; Choudhuri et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2017), CD45's contribution to kinetic proofreading may be different in the context of the native TCR-pMHC interaction.
claims.evidence: This is a caveat based on cited prior work showing size-dependence of CD45 exclusion.

claims.claim: A study with a DNA-based CAR found a delay between ligand binding and ZAP70 recruitment, implicating some kinetic proofreading effects upstream of ZAP70 recruitment.
claims.source: Our results differ from a study with a DNA-based CAR, which found a delay between ligand binding and ZAP70 recruitment, implicating some kinetic proofreading effects upstream of ZAP70 recruitment.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claims.claim: The delay between ligand binding and ZAP70 recruitment in the DNA-based CAR was related to the time needed for ligand-occupied CARs to form small clusters.
claims.source: Mechanistically, this delay was related to the time needed for ligand-occupied CARs to form small clusters, the only place where effective ZAP70 recruitment was observed.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the mechanism from prior work.

claims.claim: The putative dimeric state of the CAR used in this study versus the putative monomeric state of the DNA-based CAR could account for differences in ZAP70 recruitment kinetics.
claims.source: The putative dimeric state of our CAR (Irving and Weiss, 1991) versus the putative monomeric state of their CAR (Bhatia et al., 2005) could account for these differences.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: For cells with high CAR occupancy but low ligand binding half-life, ZAP70 recruitment is observed without high DAG levels.
claims.source: Significantly, for cells with high CAR occupancy but low ligand binding half-life, we observe ZAP70 recruitment without high DAG levels.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claims.claim: A two-step ZAP70 activation model predicts that ZAP70 can be recruited without strong downstream signaling.
claims.source: These results nicely match the prediction of a two-step ZAP70 activation model. Requiring ZAP70 to bind a phospho-ITAMs and then subsequently be phosphorylated by Lck for full activity allows cells to have significant ZAP70 recruitment without strong downstream signaling (Thill et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a model prediction supported by citation.

claims.claim: In thymocytes and peripheral T cells in vivo, ZAP70 can be recruited to the CD3zeta but not phosphorylated.
claims.source: It also matches observations of thymocytes and peripheral T cells in vivo, where ZAP70 can be recruited to the CD3zeta but not phosphorylated (van Oers et al., 1994; Madrenas et al., 1995), a prerequisite for full activity (Yan et al., 2013; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior observations.

claims.claim: The recruitment of Lck to the TCR is a key rate-limiting step in discriminating ligand binding lifetimes.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that the recruitment of Lck to the TCR is a key rate-limiting step in discriminating ligand binding lifetimes but left open whether it was mediated through Lck's phosphorylation of ITAMs or ZAP70 (Stepanek et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Lck's proofreading effects are mediated through ZAP70 phosphorylation.
claims.source: As we observe no kinetic proofreading in ZAP70 recruitment, our results suggest Lck's proofreading effects are mediated through ZAP70 phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ZAP70 recruitment shows no proofreading.

claims.claim: TCR ITAM phosphorylation is sensitive to the strength of the pMHC.
claims.source: However, TCR ITAM phosphorylation is sensitive to the strength of the pMHC (Sloan-Lancaster et al., 1994; Madrenas et al., 1997; Madrenas et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: ZAP70 recruitment may not parallel ITAM phosphorylation because both tyrosines within a single ITAM need to be phosphorylated to effectively recruit ZAP70.
claims.source: It could be that ZAP70 recruitment doesn't parallel ITAM phosphorylation(Sloan-Lancaster et al., 1994), as both tyrosines within a single ITAM need to be phosphorylated to effectively recruit ZAP70 or that parameters other than binding lifetime affect ITAM phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism supported by citation.

claims.claim: ZAP70 phosphorylation is attractive as a proofreading step because it occurs physically close to the receptor, allowing it to reset quickly upon ligand dissociation.
claims.source: ZAP70 phosphorylation is attractive as a proofreading step because it occurs physically close to the receptor, allowing it to reset quickly upon ligand dissociation. This is a central requirement of kinetic proofreading.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the requirements of kinetic proofreading.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation of Y132 on LAT is a candidate biochemical step for kinetic proofreading because of its involvement in recruiting PLCγ.
claims.source: Another candidate biochemical step could be the phosphorylation of Y132 on LAT because of its involvement in recruiting PLCγ (Paz et al., 2001; Lin and Weiss, 2001; Zhang et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations about LAT's role.

claims.claim: Lck acts as a bridge between ZAP70 and LAT.
claims.source: Lck was recently shown to act as a bridge between ZAP70 and LAT (Lo et al., 2018), suggesting that at least some fraction of LAT molecules could be tethered to phosphorylated ITAMs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claims.claim: Experiments with a CAR revealed a similar degree of kinetic proofreading as complementary experiments that measured calcium release downstream of optogenetic stimulation of the TCR.
claims.source: Additionally, our experiments with a CAR revealed a similar degree of kinetic proofreading as complementary experiments that measured calcium release downstream of optogenetic stimulation of the TCR (see Yousefi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to a complementary study cited.

claims.claim: Both DAG levels and calcium release are immediate consequences of PLCγ activity.
claims.source: As both DAG levels and calcium release are similarly situated in the signaling pathway (both being immediate consequences of PLCγ activity), it suggests that the observed kinetic proofreading is a consequence of shared signaling elements between these two systems, either at the level of the receptors and/or the proximal signaling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known signaling pathway architecture.

claims.claim: Ligand half-life discrimination is not completed entirely by the receptor (CAR or TCR) and kinetic proofreading can emerge from steps in the proximal signaling pathway.
claims.source: Considering our ZAP70 results, the most parsimonious explanation is that ligand half-life discrimination is not completed entirely by the receptor (CAR or TCR) and that kinetic proofreading can emerge from steps in the proximal signaling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the observation that proofreading occurs downstream of ZAP70 recruitment.

claims.claim: Foreign-pMHCs must signal at least 10⁴–10⁵ fold stronger than self-pMHCs given that T cells can respond to between 1–10 foreign-pMHCs in the context of ~10⁵–10⁶ self-pMHCs.
claims.source: As T cells can respond to between 1–10 foreign-pMHCs (Irvine et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2013) in the context of ~105–106 self-pMHCs (Unternaehrer et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2003; Bhardwaj et al., 1993), foreign-pMHCs must signal at least 104–105 fold stronger than self-pMHCs.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from cited quantitative data about pMHC numbers and T cell sensitivity.

claims.claim: Differences in binding half-lives between self-pMHCs and foreign-pMHCs are on the order of 10-fold.
claims.source: Given that differences in binding half-lives between self-pMHCs and foreign-pMHCs are on the order of 10-fold (Davis et al., 1998; Germain and Stefanová, 1999; Gascoigne et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2010), our observed degree proofreading can account for much, but not all, of ligand discrimination.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior kinetic measurements.

claims.claim: The observed degree of proofreading can account for much, but not all, of ligand discrimination.
claims.source: Given that differences in binding half-lives between self-pMHCs and foreign-pMHCs are on the order of 10-fold (Davis et al., 1998; Germain and Stefanová, 1999; Gascoigne et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2010), our observed degree proofreading can account for much, but not all, of ligand discrimination.
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing the amplification from n=2.7 (~5,000-fold for 10-fold difference) to the required 10⁴–10⁵ fold discrimination.

claims.claim: T cells likely use kinetic proofreading in combination with other mechanisms to fully discriminate self from non-self.
claims.source: T cells likely use kinetic proofreading in combination with other mechanisms, such as co-receptor involvement (Irvine et al., 2002), mechanical forces (Kim et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014), or signal amplification downstream of DAG (Das et al., 2009), to fully discriminate self from non-self.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinetic proofreading alone cannot account for all discrimination, supported by citations to other mechanisms.

results.result: The authors developed an optogenetic approach using the LOVTRAP system to specifically tune ligand binding half-life without altering other binding parameters. Blue light intensity controls LOV2-Zdk binding half-life from ~500 ms to 10 s while keeping the binding interface constant, thereby uncoupling half-life from mechanical stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C44, and C24 provide direct experimental evidence (Figure 2A,B) that blue light intensity tunes binding half-life across the physiological range. Claims C27-C29 establish the conceptual advantage: the binding interface remains constant, so mechanical stability is unchanged. This is a well-supported technical achievement that addresses a key limitation (C2) in the field.

results.result: LOV2 photoreversibly binds the Zdk-CAR and induces DAG accumulation in a blue-light-dependent manner. LOV2 accumulates under cells in the dark and disperses upon blue light illumination through multiple cycles without loss of potency. ZAP70 co-localizes with CAR occupancy sites while DAG shows diffuse localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are directly supported by microscopy data (Figure 1C-E, Videos 1-3, supplementary figures). The negative control (C36) confirms specificity. The temporal dynamics (C39) and spatial localization patterns (C37-C38) are consistent with known T cell signaling biology, providing validation of the system.

results.result: At constant receptor occupancy, increasing ligand binding half-life increases DAG signaling. Binding half-life predicts DAG levels well across different ligand concentrations (strong correlation), while receptor occupancy shows poor correlation with DAG. Signaling increases most for half-lives between 4-7 s.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C51-C53 are supported by rigorous analysis across multiple LOV2 concentrations at constant occupancy (Figure 3B-E, supplementary figures). The experimental design cleverly decouples occupancy from half-life. The correlation analysis is quantitative (Spearman's ρ reported). Claim C47's 4-7 s threshold agrees with prior pMHC literature, adding biological validation.

results.result: The degree of kinetic proofreading is n = 2.7 ± 0.5 (95% CI), which could amplify a 10-fold difference in ligand binding half-life into a ~5,000-fold difference in DAG levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by model fitting to experimental data (Figure 4 supplements 1-2). The model is explicitly described in Methods with appropriate statistical analysis (95% CI). Claim C55 follows mathematically from the fitted n value. However, the authors acknowledge this is a simplified model and provides a conservative lower bound on n, which is appropriately cautious.

results.result: ZAP70 recruitment shows no detectable kinetic proofreading (n ≈ 0) and depends solely on CAR occupancy, not binding half-life. Kinetic proofreading occurs downstream of ZAP70 recruitment and upstream of DAG accumulation in the proximal signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4 supplement 3) showing ZAP70 recruitment is independent of half-life. The localization of proofreading (C58, C4, C32) is a logical inference from comparing ZAP70 (no proofreading) vs DAG (proofreading). This is a key mechanistic finding that narrows down where discrimination occurs.

results.result: Longer ligand binding half-lifetimes are a key parameter for potent T cell signaling, providing direct evidence for kinetic proofreading in T cell ligand discrimination.
results.evaluation: This is the central conclusion supported by the entire experimental dataset. Claims C31 and C53 are directly supported by the DAG measurements showing half-life dependence. Claim C1 frames this as evidence for kinetic proofreading, which is justified given the quantitative modeling (C54-C55) and mechanistic localization (C56-C58).

results.result: The observed kinetic proofreading (n=2.7) can account for much but not all ligand discrimination. Given 10-fold differences in self vs foreign pMHC half-lives and the need for 10⁴-10⁵ fold discrimination, T cells likely use kinetic proofreading in combination with other mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 cite prior quantitative measurements of pMHC numbers and half-lives. Claim C82 correctly calculates that n=2.7 yields ~5,000-fold amplification for 10-fold half-life difference, which is less than the required 10⁴-10⁵ fold. Claim C83's conclusion that additional mechanisms are needed is a logical inference well-supported by citations to candidate mechanisms.

results.result: Lck's proofreading effects are likely mediated through ZAP70 phosphorylation rather than ITAM phosphorylation. Kinetic proofreading emerges from steps in the proximal signaling pathway, not solely from the receptor. Candidate steps include ZAP70 phosphorylation and LAT Y132 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is an inference from the observation that ZAP70 recruitment shows no proofreading, but this is indirect. Claims C74-C75 are explicitly speculative ("attractive," "could be"). Claim C79 is a reasonable inference but goes beyond what the data directly show. These are plausible mechanistic hypotheses that require direct experimental validation (e.g., measuring ZAP70 phosphorylation kinetics, LAT phosphorylation).

results.result: CD45 exclusion does not contribute to measurable kinetic proofreading at the level of ZAP70 recruitment in the CAR system, though its role may differ in native TCR-pMHC interactions due to size-dependence of CD45 exclusion.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 shows equal proofreading with/without anti-β2m antibody (data in Figure 4 supplement 3), supporting that CD45 exclusion is not required. Claim C62 is a reasonable inference from C56-C57. Claim C63 appropriately caveats that the CAR system may differ from native TCR, supported by citations showing size-dependence of CD45 effects.

results.result: The CAR is expressed at 62-238 × 10³ molecules per cell, comparable to native TCR (273-547 × 10³). Cells are sensitive to 40-1,200 LOV2 molecules/μm² on the bilayer, comparable to other CAR systems and slightly less sensitive than primary T cells with pMHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by quantitative flow cytometry measurements (Figure 1 supplement 4) and experimental titrations (Figure 4 supplement 2, Methods). Comparisons to literature values are appropriately cited. These characterizations validate that the system operates in a physiologically relevant range.

results.result: Cells with different receptor occupancies can have similar DAG levels when exposed to similar blue light doses. Blue light intensity finely tunes both DAG levels and receptor occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is directly observed in microscopy data (Figure 1C-E) and motivates the key experimental design. Claim C45 is demonstrated in time courses (Figure 2C, supplementary figures, Videos 6-7). These observations establish that occupancy alone does not determine signaling and that the optogenetic system provides fine control.

results.result: The CAR system shows similar kinetic proofreading as complementary TCR optogenetic experiments measuring calcium. Both DAG and calcium are downstream of PLCγ, suggesting proofreading arises from shared signaling elements.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 cites a complementary study (Yousefi et al., 2019) showing similar n values. Claim C78 correctly notes that DAG and calcium are both immediate PLCγ products, making the inference reasonable. This cross-validation between two independent optogenetic approaches strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: High CAR occupancy with short binding half-life produces ZAP70 recruitment without high DAG levels, consistent with a two-step ZAP70 activation model requiring both recruitment and phosphorylation for full activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is observed in the data. Claims C68-C69 cite prior models and observations supporting two-step ZAP70 activation. The consistency between the current observations and prior models is appropriately noted. This provides mechanistic context for understanding the uncoupling of ZAP70 recruitment from downstream signaling.

results.result: Results differ from a DNA-based CAR study that found proofreading upstream of ZAP70 recruitment. The difference may be due to the dimeric state of the current CAR versus the monomeric DNA-based CAR.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 accurately describe prior work. Claim C66 is speculative ("could account") about the mechanistic basis for differences. Without direct comparison experiments or structural characterization of the CAR oligomeric state, this remains a plausible but unvalidated hypothesis.

results.result: Fast rebinding can extend effective receptor engagement time. The optogenetic approach may reduce rebinding effects compared to altered peptide series because LOV2 is refractory to CAR binding after blue light stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by citations to prior work. Claim C49 cites 2D kinetic measurements. Claim C50 is an inference about the optogenetic system based on LOV2 properties, but this is not directly tested. The 4-7 s threshold (C47) could underestimate the true threshold if rebinding occurs, as the authors acknowledge.

results.result: Self-pMHCs outnumber foreign-pMHCs by orders of magnitude. For many receptors, occupancy drives signaling, but for T cells, low affinity pMHCs are less potent than high affinity pMHCs even at equal occupancy. More TCRs are likely bound to self-pMHC than foreign-pMHC.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior quantitative studies. These establish the biological context and motivation for why kinetic proofreading is an attractive model for T cell ligand discrimination. This is standard background knowledge in the field.

results.result: Kinetic proofreading predicts that small differences in ligand binding half-life can be amplified into large signaling differences through multiple irreversible biochemical steps that only occur while ligand is bound. This mechanism operates in DNA replication, translation, and splicing. Stimulatory pMHCs generally have longer half-lives than non-stimulatory pMHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 accurately describe the kinetic proofreading model and its precedents in other biological systems, supported by appropriate citations. Claim C15 cites multiple studies showing correlation between pMHC half-life and stimulatory capacity. This provides the theoretical framework and prior evidence motivating the current study.

results.result: Existing methods of altering ligand binding half-life (altered peptide series) simultaneously change mechanical stability because both depend on the binding interface. The TCR is mechanosensitive and foreign-pMHC can form catch bonds, making it difficult to distinguish kinetic proofreading from mechanosensing.
results.evaluation: Claim C2 states a known limitation motivating the study. Claims C17-C19 are supported by citations to prior work on TCR mechanosensitivity and catch bonds. This establishes why a new approach is needed to specifically test kinetic proofreading independent of mechanical effects.

results.result: The CAR approach is simpler than the TCR, easier to engineer, medically relevant, and bypasses early signaling steps like CD4/CD8 coreceptor involvement, allowing focus on the shared downstream pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are general characterizations of CARs supported by citations. Claim C30 correctly notes that CARs lack coreceptors, which is a known difference from native TCRs. This justifies the choice of experimental system and acknowledges its limitations relative to native TCR signaling.

results.result: Recent 2D measurements show a larger range of pMHC binding affinities than previously measured, suggesting there may not be as large an excess of self-pMHC bound to TCR and raising questions about the magnitude of kinetic proofreading needed.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 is supported by citation to a specific study (Huang et al., 2010). This provides context for why quantifying the degree of kinetic proofreading (n) is important and timely, as newer measurements suggest the discrimination problem may differ from classical estimates.

results.result: T cells on supported lipid bilayers can display ligand-independent signaling due to CD45 exclusion from the close membrane apposition, favoring ITAM phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by citations to prior work. This acknowledges a potential confounding factor in the experimental system and provides context for the control experiments (C61) showing that the main results are not dependent on this effect.

results.result: Lck recruitment to the TCR is a rate-limiting step in discriminating ligand half-lives. TCR ITAM phosphorylation is sensitive to pMHC strength. ZAP70 recruitment may not parallel ITAM phosphorylation. Lck bridges ZAP70 and LAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C72, and C76 are supported by citations to prior work. Claim C73 is speculative but appropriately caveated. These provide mechanistic context from the literature for interpreting the current findings about where proofreading occurs in the pathway.
